ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns, though presentations are long, highly structured monologues followed by brief audience exchanges. The opening is loose and chatty, with greetings, technical checks, side conversations, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), and occasional overlap or abrupt handoffs; transcription-like false starts, repetitions, and self-corrections are common. Participants use frequent hedges and softeners—“I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know,” “I guess,” “it could be”—especially when speculating or framing limitations. The tone is professionally informal: speakers use polished scientific framing during talks but switch to warm, conversational praise and lightly humorous remarks in discussion. Questions are usually prefaced with compliments or disclaimers such as “great talk,” “quick question,” or “naive question,” then unfold as multipart, exploratory prompts. Challenges are indirect and curiosity-driven rather than adversarial, often phrased as requests for clarification or alternative possibilities; speakers respond expansively, acknowledge uncertainty, and build on the question rather than rebutting it.

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Protecting outdoor workers from wildfire smoke when air-quality alerts arrive after the shift has already started.

speakers.name: Dr. Marisol Vega
speakers.background: An air-quality scientist with 12 years of experience in wildfire-smoke exposure assessment for rural communities. She has managed county-scale monitoring projects using regulatory PM2.5 data, low-cost sensor co-location, satellite aerosol products, and smoke-plume forecast systems. Her recent work has examined indoor-outdoor particulate infiltration in schools, community centers, and agricultural facilities during smoke episodes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the pilot as an operational exposure-classification problem: the team needs a defensible, timely trigger that integrates observed PM2.5 with forward-looking plume information rather than treating either source as sufficient alone. She is focused on quantifying alert-feed latency, local spatial representativeness, and the actual protection provided by candidate clean-air spaces through infiltration measurements. She sees the initial protocol as a testable decision workflow whose thresholds and routing rules must follow environmental characterization, not assumptions.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Aaron Patel
speakers.background: An occupational and environmental epidemiologist with 8 years of experience designing field studies of short-term air-pollution exposure and respiratory health. He has worked with repeated symptom surveys, personal exposure monitoring, urgent-care and emergency-department encounter data, and quasi-experimental pilot designs. Much of his prior work has been in urban settings, and he is adapting those measurement approaches to agricultural and contingent-worker populations.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Approaches the pilot through measurement validity and causal interpretation. He wants the team to pre-specify feasible exposure metrics and a short follow-up for acute respiratory symptoms, while developing transparent criteria for identifying plausibly smoke-related respiratory visits. He is especially concerned that heat, physical exertion, baseline respiratory disease, and differential access to care could distort apparent associations. He will press the group to distinguish feasibility and signal detection in a pilot from an effectiveness claim.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Lucía Hernández, PhD
speakers.background: A medical and labor sociologist with 14 years of experience conducting bilingual qualitative research with farmworkers, day laborers, and immigrant worker organizations in the western United States. Her methods include rapid ethnography, semi-structured interviews, workplace communication mapping, and participatory protocol design. She has studied how piece-rate pay, contractor arrangements, immigration concerns, transportation constraints, and supervisor discretion shape whether workers can act on health guidance.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats an alert as a social and employment event rather than merely an information event. She will ask how a mid-shift message reaches workers across crews and contractors, who can authorize a break or relocation, and whether following instructions could cost workers pay, future shifts, or standing with a supervisor. She prioritizes learning what English- and Spanish-language materials, trusted messengers, channels, and accessibility supports are necessary to include seasonal, informal, and day-labor workers. She views worker feasibility findings as a prerequisite for any protocol that claims to be practical.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

benchmark_task: Give a meeting planning research next steps with 2-4 disciplines represented. The evaluated AI must map tasks to disciplines consistently with the discussion.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting planning research next steps with 2-4 disciplines represented. The evaluated AI must map tasks to disciplines consistently with the discussion.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting with one environmental scientist, one epidemiologist, and one sociologist. Establish that the team will pursue a pilot rather than make claims about effectiveness yet. The environmental scientist should identify the need to define an alert trigger using both PM2.5 observations and plume forecasts, assess the lag in the existing alert feed, and characterize likely clean-air locations through indoor-outdoor infiltration measurements. The epidemiologist should identify the need to specify exposure and health outcome measures, including a short respiratory-symptom follow-up and criteria for identifying smoke-related respiratory visits while accounting for heat as a confounder. The sociologist should identify the need to learn how workers receive mid-shift messages, whether workers can safely act on them without losing pay or shifts, and what language/accessibility arrangements are needed for informal and day-labor workers. The group should agree that the first operational protocol cannot be finalized until the environmental trigger assessment and worker feasibility findings are available. Assign concrete next steps, owners, and dependencies. Do not resolve the numerical PM2.5 threshold, the final outcome definition, or the participating employer list during the meeting; leave these as items requiring the assigned work.

agreed_scope.decision: Conduct a pilot to develop and test the feasibility of a mid-shift smoke alert-response protocol, not to make a definitive effectiveness claim.
agreed_scope.population: Outdoor workers in the selected agricultural county, including seasonal, informal, and day-labor workers.
agreed_scope.protocol_goal: Provide a feasible response when smoke conditions worsen after a shift has begun, potentially including relocation to cleaner indoor space, modified duties, breaks, or a stop-work option.

tasks: Compare county PM2.5 monitor data, available local or portable sensor options, and regional smoke-plume forecasts to propose candidate real-time alert triggers.
Document the timing and lag of the current alert feed relative to observed smoke conditions during representative smoke events.
Measure or estimate indoor-outdoor PM2.5 infiltration at candidate clean-air locations and report which sites could plausibly reduce exposure.
task_assignments.deliverable: A trigger-options memo and clean-air-site exposure characterization.
dependencies: The operational protocol must wait for the trigger-options memo and clean-air-site characterization.

tasks: Draft a measurement plan for worker smoke exposure and short-term respiratory symptoms following alert events.
Propose a case definition and data source for smoke-related respiratory visits, while distinguishing the pilot's feasible surveillance outcomes from a definitive causal health-effect study.
Specify how heat will be measured and addressed as a confounder in the pilot analysis.
task_assignments.deliverable: A draft outcome, case-definition, and confounding-control plan.
dependencies: Final outcome definitions remain pending review of feasible symptom and visit data sources.

tasks: Conduct formative interviews or brief fieldwork with workers, labor intermediaries, and employers about how mid-shift alerts can reach workers and which communication channels are trusted.
Assess whether workers can take breaks, move indoors, change tasks, or stop work without retaliation, lost pay, or loss of future shifts.
Develop recommendations for English and Spanish materials and for recruitment and communication approaches that include informal and day-labor workers.
task_assignments.deliverable: A worker and employer feasibility brief, including communication and language-access recommendations.
dependencies: The operational protocol must wait for findings about safe worker actions, communication channels, and language access.

coordination_decisions: The environmental trigger assessment and the sociological feasibility findings will jointly determine the first operational alert-response protocol.
The epidemiologic measurement plan will be aligned with the resulting protocol so that alert timing, response uptake, exposure, heat, and short-term health measures can be linked.
A cross-disciplinary review will occur after the three initial deliverables are complete to select the protocol, finalize measures, and identify participating employers.
unresolved_items: The numerical PM2.5 threshold and exact forecast criterion for triggering an alert.
The final definition of smoke-related respiratory visits and the final set of short-term health outcomes.
The participating employer list and which worksites will be enrolled.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. Before we get into it, I’m hoping we can leave today with a clearer sense of what we need to learn from workers and crew leads before we treat an alert protocol as workable, especially once people are already out in the fields. Maybe we can do a quick update—quick updates first?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: That would be really useful. On my side, I want us to resist naming a trigger rule before we know what the monitor and plume product actually buy us locally. Last season's timing may tell us the alert feed is already behind the exposure curve. And for the indoor sites, I'm especially interested in which ones workers could realistically reach mid-shift, because a nominal clean-air room- if it's forty minutes away, that's not an intervention.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: Even if a site is close on a map, I’d want to know if a crew lead can actually release people, whether there’s transport, and what happens to piece-rate earnings during that time. Marisol, when the plume forecast is worsening, do you have a sense yet of how much lead time it might give us over the monitor?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Not yet, and I don’t want to overpromise. I’m expecting the plume product might give us a useful directional window, maybe several hours in some transport regimes, but it’ll miss or mis-time local surface concentrations. So I need to reconstruct last season’s events against the county series and measure that lead or lag explicitly. I’m also checking whether a few colocated portable sensors would show field-level gradients the county monitor can’t see, and if they do...

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: Mm, that field variation worries me.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Patel
transcript.text: That variation matters for what we can honestly measure. Marisol, when you do that reconstruction, could you look at the distribution of monitor-to-plume timing, not just an average lead? For the pilot, I'd want to log the forecast, the monitor crossing, and the actual crew response separately. Otherwise a null symptom signal could just- it could mean the alert arrived after the relevant exposure window.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I’ll treat those as three distinct timestamps, and I’ll give us the full event-level distribution, especially the bad tail, not just the median. And I also want to flag when the county monitor is plausibly unrepresentative of a crew’s location, because a clean-looking central-site trace could otherwise make the response look late when it’s really- when it’s actually a spatial mismatch.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: I’d be cautious about calling any response late until we know what the crew actually heard and who had discretion to act. A central monitor, a forecast, a supervisor’s text, and a crew lead- those are four different events from the worker’s side, you know? I’d like our fieldwork to capture those timestamps too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: That distinction is really important. I can keep the environmental timestamps alongside the communication chain instead of trying to collapse them into one "alert time," and then we can see whether a miss was forecast performance, monitor representativeness, dissemination, or a genuinely infeasible response. For the field locations, Lucía, I’d really value a short list of places crews could actually get to within, say, a break-length, break-length window, not just sites that exist.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: I can build that list through brief field visits instead of assuming the health department's site list is usable. I'd look at where crews are, how they get around, and whether a room feels safe to enter mid-shift. And I'd test the English and Spanish alert language with workers and crew leads, because the same instruction can land very differently as a text than when someone repeats it in person.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Patel
transcript.text: That would help a lot, because for the symptom piece, I need to know what follow-up channel is realistic after the shift. Lucía, do you have an early hunch whether a very short text or WhatsApp check-in the next morning would reach day-labor workers, or would it, um, need to come through the crew lead? I'm trying not to build an outcome measure around a response pattern that's mostly about phone access or pay pressure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s a real concern.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: I don't think it can be just one channel. A WhatsApp or text the next morning may work for some people, but for day laborers and seasonal crews it may be intermittent or shared, or they may just ignore it if it feels connected to the employer. I'd want to ask workers whether a community intermediary feels more trustworthy. And Aaron, would voice responses or assisted completion still give you something interpretable?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Patel
transcript.text: I think so, as long as we treat the mode as part of the measurement process instead of pretending it’s neutral. We could keep the core symptom items really short and identical, cough, wheeze, shortness of breath, throat or eye irritation, and record whether it was self-completed, voice, or assisted. Then we can see whether responses differ by channel. I’d also want a baseline respiratory-history question early on, but not anything that turns the check-in into a survey.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: That sounds workable, especially if the assisted option is clearly separate from the employer. Otherwise people may answer in ways that feel safer rather than more accurate. I’d also ask in the formative conversations who they’d actually accept help from. A promotor/a, a worker organization, maybe a clinic outreach person. It may- it could differ pretty sharply by crew arrangement.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: That mode field is useful on the environmental side too, because we can line up the symptom window with the response timestamp instead of acting like everyone had the same intervention. Aaron, if smoke goes up partway through a shift, is next-morning reporting still close enough to interpret if we log when they moved indoors, or would you want an end-of-shift check as...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Patel
transcript.text: I'd lean toward a really brief end-of-shift check, if we can keep it low burden, and then a next-morning follow-up for symptoms that emerge or persist overnight. But I don't think we should treat either one as a clean acute-effect measure until we capture heat and task intensity that day. The throat and eye reports I saw last summer were weirdly high on hot, only moderately smoky days. We can use the pilot to see whether those windows and channels actually give us usable within-event signal.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: And I’d be careful that an end-of-shift check doesn’t become another thing workers have to do when they’re trying to get transport or secure tomorrow’s work. In the field conversations, I can ask what moment is least risky and most, uh, realistic, and whether we can capture heat and task intensity with a couple of plain-language items instead of asking people to reconstruct the whole day.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Patel
transcript.text: A couple of plain-language items may be enough, like whether the work felt light, moderate, or very strenuous, and whether they spent much of the shift in direct sun. I'd rather measure those imperfectly than leave heat and exertion completely folded into the smoke signal. We can also pair that with weather-station temperature or heat index, assuming there's one close enough to the crews, crews.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: Mm. And the heat question needs to include whether they could get water, shade, or a break, because those aren't just individual conditions. They depend on the crew and the supervisor. I don't think we need to settle the exact items today, but that's something I'd put in the worker feasibility conversations, whether those questions feel answerable, answerable at all after a piece-rate day.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Patel
transcript.text: I’d keep those as context items, not try to turn them into a precise heat-exposure score. For the analysis, we need the ambient heat index plus those worker-reported conditions, then see if the symptom pattern is even separable from smoke in this small pilot. Otherwise, we’ll be calling irritation a PM effect when it may just be a brutal hot day.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: From the exposure side, that means we should keep heat as a parallel condition, not try to make the PM trigger explain every high-symptom day. I’m also thinking the clean-air-site checks need temperature and, I lost my train of thought there, door traffic and HVAC operating status logged alongside indoor and outdoor PM. Two rooms that looked comparable behaved completely differently for us last season.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: And I’d add one social check to that site log, like who controls the door and whether workers can enter without a supervisor calling ahead. A room can have great filtration and still be unusable if people feel they need permission, or worry they’ll be marked as difficult for leaving the crew. I’ll make sure the site visits ask that directly.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yes—usability is part of the exposure pathway, not an add-on.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Patel
transcript.text: That’s why I’d define uptake as more than just, "the site was available." We should log whether a worker was offered the option, whether they could enter, and how long they actually spent there. Otherwise, any exposure or symptom comparison is basically uninterpretable. I’ll keep the outcome plan focused on feasibility and signal detection, not an effectiveness claim, until we know what those logs and the follow-ups can support.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: That feels like the right stopping point. We should not call this an employer protocol until we know whether workers are actually offered the response, able to use it, and safe using it. I’ll frame the formative piece around that whole chain, the message, authority, transport, pay risk, and follow-up channel, and come back with a feasibility brief before we lock the first version, because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I think we've covered what we needed for today, and I know we're at the hard stop. Thanks, everyone. Let's reconnect once the feasibility and environmental— once those pieces have had a little time to take shape.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Patel
transcript.text: Sounds good. Take care, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Lucía Hernández, PhD
transcript.text: Thanks, both. Bye for now.
